title: Pelagic mizer model
text:
Overview
The model presented here is an updated version of that used in Woodworth-Jefcoats et al. (2019). This updated version:
This model is a tool meant to generally capture the Hawaiʻi-based longline fisheries and the dynamics of the ecosystem supporting them in a manner that allows for simulation testing. It is designed to complement assessments, not substitute for them.
To get the most out of this site, it’s recommended that you also visit the linked RMarkdown scripts in the accompanying repo.

title: Pelagic mizer model
text:
What’s here
This site takes you through the system that’s being modeled and discusses the data used in parameterizing the model. It provides an overview of the calibration/validation process, including discussing which parameters were changed from their default values and why. It then discusses several possible approaches to improving the model’s fit to observed catch, walks through a brief guide to running this particular mizer model, and offers some ideas for simulations. Citations for all references are provided.

title: Pelagic mizer model
text:
Resources
The mizer site includes model documentation, tutorials, and more. If you’re unfamiliar with mizer, start there and then come back to this specific model. The sizespectrum GitHub site includes a number of repositories hosting extensions of the mizer model. And, mizerExperimental has additional functionality that users might find helpful.

title: 1  Fisheries modeled
text:
This model is built to capture the Hawaiʻi-based longline fishery, which is actually two fisheries: a tuna fishery and a swordfish fishery. The tuna fishery targets bigeye tuna (Thunnus obesus) and is often referred to as the “deep-set fishery” because it sets its hooks deeper in the water column (100–400 m) to capture bigeye tuna when they’re foraging at depth during the daytime (Bigelow et al. (2006)). As the name suggests, the swordfish fishery targets swordfish (Xiphias gladius) and is often referred to as the “shallow-set fishery” because it sets it hooks closer to the surface (upper 100 m) to capture swordfish when they’re foraging at night (Bigelow et al. (2006)). The deep-set fishery is by far the larger of the two fisheries by any measure (e.g., vessels, hooks, catch, revenue). It operates year-round while the swordfish fishery is seasonal and concentrates its effort in the winter. The fisheries also have different spatial footprints, as seen in Figure 1.1. Broadly, the longline fishery fishes in an area roughly bounded by the dateline, the 15\(\degree\)C sea surface temperature isotherm (Locarnini et al. (2024)), the western edge of the US EEZ off California, and low-oxygen waters in the eastern tropical Pacific (which we define as waters within 200 m of the surface having less than 2.1 ml l-1 O2; Garcia et al. (2024)).

title: 2  Data used
text:
2.1 Fisheries data
This model is the beneficiary of several existing datasets, which are accessible to varying degrees.
All information about this fishery comes from Pacific Islands Region Observer Program data. Observers are mandated to cover all shallow-set swordfish trips and 20% of deep-set bigeye tuna trips (NOAA Fisheries (2026)). They measure a plethora of operational details including the time, location, and amount of all effort set (with effort being the number of hooks). They also record all catch regardless of commercial value. Finally, since February 2006, observers have maintained the protocol of measuring the length of every third fish caught1. These factors combine to make observer data our best source for understanding how many of what size of each species fish are caught. The size part is particularly helpful for mizer.
We use data from February 2006 through December 2024 to encompass the period during which a consistent measurement protocol was in place, ending with the most recent complete year available at time of download. Observer data are subject to confidentiality of information requirements under the Magnuson–Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson–Stevens Act or MSA) and are not available to the public except in summary aggregate form.

title: 2  Data used
text:
2.2 Fish data
Diet data for the species modeled here came largely from Barnes et al. (2008). Data were filtered to retain pelagic habitats and species representative of the model domain and species composition. Species-specific diet information was available for bigeye tuna, swordfish, yellowfin tuna, and albacore tuna (see below for this species). For the remaining species, filtered data were grouped to identify generic values for teleosts and sharks. Data for albacore tuna from Barnes et al. (2008) were combined with albacore tuna diet data from Pinnegar et al. (2015) and Goñi (2014). These data informed feeding kernel parameters.
Information for remaining parameters was taken from the literature (see Chapter 3). When data for needed parameters wasn’t in the literature, we turned to FishLife (Thorson et al. (2023)) and FishBase (Froese & Pauly (2026)).
All data described in this section are publicly available and can be accessed using links included here and by following information in the citations.

title: 3  Species parameters
text:
Gathering needed species parameters is probably the biggest job in building a mizer model, particularly if you’re working with poorly understood species in a data-poor region. Working with a team makes the job easier1. It also helps that mizer will estimate many parameters for you based on sound science. See their site for more.
To start, we gathered the parameters listed in Table 3.1 by consulting the corresponding references listed in Table 3.2. While these tables look nice and tidy, there was ample background work involved. Our team had a shared Google doc where we noted parameters and left helpful feedback for one another. The final parameters were added to a data frame using a script, although you could absolutely do this step in the spreadsheet editor of your choice (and it would probably be easier).
In Table 3.1, the NA values for weight-related parameters (e.g., w_mat, w_max) indicate weights that are converted from lengths using the a and b parameters. NA values for a and b parameters indicate sexually dimorphic species. In these cases, weights are calculated for each sex and then averaged. NA values for length-related parameters (e.g., l_mat, l_max) indicate species for which the corresponding weights were available without conversion. These NA values all carry through to Table 3.2.
In Table 3.2, default indicates parameters that were estimated following the prior methodology:
Each species’ minimum and maximum depths (depth_min and depth_max, respectively) were used by a script to build the interaction matrix (Table 3.3) based on vertical overlap (see the original model for more details). These depth ranges were typical depth ranges, not record observations, because we want species’ typical overlap.

Note that both pomfret and escolar are species complexes due to changes in observer reporting over time. We leaned towards drawing upon references for the dominant species in each group wherever possible.

title: 4  Fishing parameters
text:
In mizer fishing mortality (F) is the product of selectivity (S), catchability (Q), and effort (E), which operate over gears (g), species (i), and size (w): \[
\begin{align}
F_i = S_{g,i,w} \times Q_{g,i} \times E_g
\end{align}
\]
Note that in mizer size is body weight in grams unless otherwise specified.
We’ll start with effort (E), which is specific to gear type. For this model, the two gear types are DeepSet and ShallowSet. To inform this parameter for each gear, we looked at the proportion of total longline effort (hooks set) each gear type deployed over the period from February 2006 through December 2024, pooled (see Chapter 2):

DeepSet Effort: 0.985
ShallowSet Effort: 0.015

Catchability (Q) is specific to both gear and species. To approximate this as best we can, we use the fishing mortality estimates from stock assessments in place of catchability, applying them equally to both gears. When assessments provided time-varying estimates, we averaged across time (time series) or chose the block of time most representative of the period covered by our data (time blocks). When multiplied by effort (E) and summed across gears (g), this results in fishing mortality (F) that’s equal to the assessment estimates. For unassessed species, we use a default value of Q = 0.2. See Table 3.1 and Table 3.2 in Chapter 3 for estimates and their sources.
Selectivity (S) was informed by observer data (see Chapter 2). We used mizer’s sigmoid_weight selectivity function and set sigmoidal_weight to the smallest size that experiences at least 25% as much catch (in number of fish caught) at the size that sees the greatest catch and sigmoidal_sigma as the number of size classes that experience at least 1% as much catch as the size that sees the greatest catch. An example of these values for bigeye tuna are shown in Figure 4.1 below. When determining these values, we binned sizes to match those used in our mizer model (see Chapter 7). You can view our code for identifying these values here.
Fishing-related parameters, or as mizer calls them, gear parameters, are summarized in Table 4.1. Species-specific fishing mortality at size is presented in Figure 4.2 below.

title: 5  Calibration and Diagnostic Evaluation
text:
The previous sections present the final parameters that we settled on after much work and adjusting. The process by which these came together involved quite a bit of iteration, particularly setting the selectivity parameters.
We have elected to fit our modeled catch-at-size to observed catch-at-size. This is the best, most comprehensive information we have about the system we’re modeling. While this approach doesn’t quite fit the bill for validation, it’s the best we can do with what we have and offers a reasonable calibration approach.
Figures Figure 5.1 and Figure 5.2 below show a variety of selectivity parameter permutations we tested and their resulting significant (p < 0.05) correlation coefficients. Modeled and observed catch-at-size was compared and figures were generated with this code. Black lines represent observed catch at size (with circles used for sharks because their lengths are reported in feet rather than cm, which leads to otherwise blocky plots). Colors represent different parameter choices as described below the figures.
In addition to trialing different thresholds for sigmoidal_weight and sigmoidal_sigma we also tested several values for kappa which is a parameter that informs initial abundances. In the end, we kept the default value (1011) because it resulted in catch magnitudes that most closely matched observed catch.

text: This implies that our system is not food limited, which is interesting to think about. title: 6  Fit Improvement Options
text:
6.1 Improving modeled spectra
The model presented here offers an improvement over Woodworth-Jefcoats et al. (2019) in that it:
We’ve taken a consistent approach to parameterizing all modeled species and stopped short of taking any species-specific steps to improve the model. That said, there are still ways the model could be improved. We discuss a few options here.
There are four species for which the size spectra fail to decrease at the largest body sizes: mahi mahi, wahoo, swordfish, and blue marlin. You can see this in Figure 6.1 below. It may help to zoom in and reposition the figure.
Figure 6.1: Steady state biomass spectra
The likeliest reason for this behavior is that these species don’t experience enough predation mortality. These four species have the smallest total interaction with other species (Table 3.3) by virtue of their depth range parameters (Table 3.1). One way to address this would be to increase external mortality for these four species. In mizer, external mortality covers all sources of mortality that aren’t explicitly modeled: predation by species that aren’t included (e.g., cetaceans), capture by fisheries that aren’t included, disease, environmental stress, etc.
In mizer, the default approach to calculating species-specific external mortality, \(\mu\), is effectively: \[
\begin{align}
\mu = 0.6 w_{max}^{-0.25}
\end{align}
\] Below is one approach to using external mortality to capture unmodeled predation on mahi mahi, wahoo, swordfish, and blue marlin.
# Initial matrix: 0 for all sizes of all species
ext_mort <- matrix(0, nrow = length(sp), ncol = length(w),
                   dimnames = list("species" = c(sp), 
                                   "w" = c(w)))

# First, fill with default values
for (s in seq(1, length(sp), 1)) {
  ext_mort[s,] <- 0.6 * w_max[s]^-0.25
}

# Identify the rows for our species
idx <- which(sp == "MahiMahi" | 
             sp == "Swordfish" |
             sp == "Wahoo" | 
             sp == "BlueMarlin")

# Loop through them and set external mortality an order of magnitude higher
# for our species
for (r in idx) {
  ext_mort[r,] <- 10 * (0.6 * w_max[r]^-0.25)
}

# Turn it into a data frame
ext_mort <- as.data.frame(ext_mort)

# Save things
write.csv(ext_mort, here("Pelagic_external_mortality_10x.csv"), row.names = TRUE, col.names = TRUE)
When you run mizer (see Chapter 7), you’d then load the external mortality in the same way other parameters are loaded:
# Load (along with other parameters)
pelagic_external_mortality <- as.matrix(read.csv(here("Pelagic_external_mortality_10x.csv"), row.names = 1))
And attach the external mortality after creating a newMultispeciesParams() object called pelagic_params (again, see Chapter 7):
pelagic_params <- setExtMort(pelagic_params,
                             ext_mort = pelagic_external_mortality)
We found that this approach improved the fit for four species in question (Figure 6.2 and Figure 6.3). However, we haven’t included this in the workflow outlined because the approach is subjective (level of increased mortality) and species-specific and therefore might not be appropriate for all applications.

title: 6  Fit Improvement Options
text:
6.2 Improving catch-at-size
As we can see in Figure 6.2 and Figure 6.3, improving the behavior of the spectra for the four species with poor ones improved their correlation with observed catch-at-size. Another way to achieve this, and to improve the fits for some other species (e.g., shortfin mako sharks) would be to increase the level of fishing mortality they experience.
In the examples shown here, we changed the catchability value (and thus F) for shortfin mako shark from 0.018 to 0.2. This improved the correlation coefficients for both the deep-set and shallow-set catch-at-size such that were significant (p < 0.05) and greater than that of several other species. Similar results were obtained for other species when we experimented with increasing fishing mortality systematically for all species. Something to think about when considering Chapter 8.






Figure 6.2: Comparison of observed and modeled deep-set catch at size under different approaches to fit improvement.









Figure 6.3: Comparison of observed and modeled deep-set catch at size under different approaches to fit improvement.

title: 6  Fit Improvement Options
text:
6.3 Improving life history parameters
Because mizer is a size structured model, the parameters for weight-at-maturity, w_mat, and maximum weight, w_max, are particularly important. These values are used to inform processes such as reproduction and natural mortality. Confirming that there aren’t better estimates available, and updating the parameters as new science comes to light, would likely improve the model.

title: 6  Fit Improvement Options
text:
6.4 Improving predation
The species in this model are nearly all apex predators. The limited diet studies available suggest that they primarily eat species other than each other. For this reason, we extend the background resource for the full size range of fish modeled. As a result, most of the predation is of the background resource. While this is probably realistic, it does mean that there’s very little in the model in the way of predator-prey interactions. Changing one species has little effect on other species. This could be changed by rethinking how predation is modeled. For example, the maximum size of the background resource could be reduced, mid-trophic level species could be added to the model, or the interaction matrix could be approached differently.

title: 6  Fit Improvement Options
text:
6.5 Improving fishing mortality
We use fishing mortality estimates from stock assessments where possible. But the footprints of these assessments extend beyond the footprints of the fisheries we represent in the model. We base our approach on both the minimal international effort where the Hawaiʻi-based fleets operate and on the likelihood that the footprint modeled is large enough to be representative of the full assessment areas. That said, there’s room for improvement in how international fisheries in particular are accounted for. Here, we discuss two possible approaches.
It would be straightforward to add additional international deep-set and shallow-set longline fleets parameterized identically to the existing domestic fleets. The balance of effort across the fleets could likely be gathered from publicly accessible international fisheries data. Validating the modeled catch would be challenging, though, given the confidential nature of the needed international data.
Our model also omits explicit representation of Pacific purse seine fleets. These fleets contribute to the mortality of small, young individuals of the species in our model. It’s possible that capturing this size-specific mortality on immature individuals would improve their model fit.

title: 6  Fit Improvement Options
text:
6.6 Which approach to take?
Whether and how you improve the model depends on your application. In general, it seems prudent to go with the approach that requires the least amount of subjective adjustment yet still results in a model that’s equal to your questions.




Woodworth-Jefcoats, P. A., Blanchard, J. L., & Drazen, J. C. (2019). Relative Impacts of Simultaneous Stressors on a Pelagic Marine Ecosystem. Frontiers in Marine Science, 6, 383. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2019.00383

title: 7  Running mizer
text:
This section walks you through running mizer using the parameters provided for Hawaiʻi-based longline fisheries. We note that when building the model as described in the previous sections it was necessary to run the model throughout the build process to identify challenges and access parameters. For example, when binning observed catch-at-size (see Chapter 4), we had to run mizer in order to extract the size bins. All this is to say, while we present things here as a straightforward unidirectional workflow, know that building and working with your own model will be iterative.
Mizer runs in R. We recommend using RStudio or a similar platform, simply for ease of use.
If you haven’t already, install mizer:

install.packages("mizer")

Load the package into your R session:

library(mizer)

Next up, you’ll need to load the parameter files and interaction matrix. The code here assumes that you’ve set up an R project that matches the structure of our repository. If you set things up differently, you’ll need to adjust the file paths accordingly.

pelagic_species_params <- read_csv(here("Pelagic_params.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
pelagic_gear_params <- read.csv(here("Pelagic_gear_params_25_1.csv"), row.names = 1)
pelagic_interaction <- read.csv(here("Pelagic_interaction.csv"), row.names = 1)

We added catchability to the species parameters because it made it easier to track the references we used. It also allowed us to easily add them to the gear parameters. We’re going to remove that column now, just to avoid any possible confusion down the line.

pelagic_species_params <- pelagic_species_params |>
  mutate(catchability = NULL)

We also need to define fishing effort (E) (see Chapter 4):

effort <- c(DeepSet = 0.985, ShallowSet = 0.015)

Now, we’re ready to set up the model for use. Exciting! We’re going to create a multi-species model with our parameters, plus some adjustments discussed in Chapter 5:

pelagic_params <- newMultispeciesParams(species_params = pelagic_species_params,
                                        gear_params = pelagic_gear_params,
                                        interaction = pelagic_interaction,
                                        initial_effort = effort,
                                        n = 0.75, p = 0.75,
                                        w_pp_cutoff = 455400)

No h provided for some species, so using age at maturity to calculate it.
No ks column so calculating from critical feeding level.
Using z0 = z0pre * w_max ^ z0exp for missing z0 values.
Using f0, h, lambda, kappa and the predation kernel to calculate gamma.


Notice that we received a message about some assumptions the model made based on the information we did and didn’t give it. This step created a full set of parameters that mizer will use to run simulations. To look at the species parameters, for example, use pelagic_params@species_params. You can use similar syntax to take a look at the other parameters. The mizer site offers extensive descriptions of the parameters and discusses this function in detail. It’s worth reading carefully to better understand this step.
The next step is to run the model to a steady state:

pelagic_steady <- steady(pelagic_params)

Convergence was achieved in 64.5 years.


The default time allowed for this is 100 years, but you can extend that if if needed: steady(pelagic_params, t_max = 500) would allow 500 years. Note that while we were building our model early iterations of this step resulted in various warnings that led us to reexamine parameters. For example, larger values of kappa led to warnings about unrealistic values for erepro. We recommend turning to mizer’s extensive documentation if you’re encountering errors while building your own model. If you encounter errors using the parameters we provided, please open an issue to let us know.
At this point, you can take a look at the size spectra of your steady-state model in Figure 7.1.

plotlySpectra(pelagic_steady, power = 2, total = TRUE)







Figure 7.1: Steady-state model spectra (note that the “Total” line mostly covers up the “Resource” line)




A full list of plotting options is available in the mizer documentation.
Note that when running to a steady state, mizer recalculates some parameters. To see what parameters are being used you can take a similar approach to that used above (pelagic_steady@species_params).
You’re now ready to run a simulation. The details of your simulation are entirely up to you and your collaborators (we offer some ideas in Chapter 8). Here, we’ll do a simple 100-year run where nothing changes. It’s not terribly exciting (or it shouldn’t be), but it does show you how to get started. Note that we’re running this simulation at a monthly time step (dt = 1/12). A temporal discretization of similar magnitude is recommended if you forego the default value of 0.1.

pelagic_sim <- project(pelagic_steady, effort = effort, t_max = 100, dt = 1/12)

Here’s how to generate a simple summary view of your simulation. See the mizer documentation for a full list of what you can view.

plot(pelagic_sim)







Figure 7.2: Summary plot for a mizer simulation

title: 8  Possible model applications
text:
8.1 Testing hypothetical future fishing scenarios
The information provided here is only the foundation for simulations. There are endless scenarios that could be modeled. Here, we discuss a few.
Mizer allows time-varying fishing effort in simulations. To do this, you need to create a data frame where each row is a time step and each column is one of the fishing gears you set up in your parameters. If you want to introduce a new fishery at some point, you’d need to include it in your parameters and set the initial effort to 0. Subsequent effort would also be 0 until the time point when you want to introduce the fishery.
Some possible questions that may be interesting in this region include:

title: 8  Possible model applications
text:
What happens if the balance of effort between deep-set and shallow-set sectors changes?
What would happen if international competition increased or decreased? (This would require creating and parameterizing an additional international fleet.)
How might increased or decreased purse seine effort affect the food web and modeled fisheries? (This would require creating and parameterizing an additional purse seine fleet.)

title: 8  Possible model applications
text:
8.2 Hindcasting, forecasting, and projecting
A handy thing about mizer is that, while it was originally developed to examine the effects of fishing mortality, you can extend it to incorporate environmental effects on fish.
Functionality exists to drive the background resource with either satellite remotely sensed or modeled data. The background resource is essentially the plankton community and it effectively limits how much food is available to all larger body sizes (i.e., modeled fish species). We’ve added code for each of these approaches in our repository. Functionality also exists to incorporate the effects of ocean temperature on fish through using the therMizer extension. To use therMizer you need to know or estimate species’ thermal tolerance limits and have a source of ocean temperature data. Thermal tolerance limits can be found in the literature in tagging studies and in databases like FishBase.
It could be interesting to use data about the past (empirical or modeled) to replicate past catch and, subsequently, forecast future catch. For future environmental conditions you could use climatological data or modeled seasonal forecast data. You can also use earth system model output to inform climate- based projections.

title: 8  Possible model applications
text:
8.3 Other sources of mortality
Marine food webs are affected by forces beyond climate and fishing. For example, deep-sea mining could affect fish mortality. Ocean acidification may affect fish both directly through their physiology and indirectly through their habitat. You could create a function to capture a specific source of mortality and use mizer’s built-in setRateFunction to incorporate it into your scenario. Note that this function allows you to change any rate function. So, for example, you could incorporate the affects of changing oxygen concentrations on predation rates.

title: 8  Possible model applications
section: 8.4 Food limitation and other ecological theories
text:
8.4 Food limitation and other ecological theories
The results of this model are sensitive to what’s decided about food limitation. If the system isn’t food limited, then effects on the background resource will have limited effect on the fish. If the system is food limited, then effects on the background resource will have clear effects on the fish. And to some degree one has to make an assumption of food limitation to pursue some of the ideas suggested above. Because mizer is based on robust yet simple ecological theory, it is straightforward to test this and other competing assumptions. One could also use mizer to explore other theoretical ecological questions, such as the degree to which ecosystems behave like economies and vice versa (e.g., Vermeij & Leigh (2011))

title: 8  Possible model applications
text:
8.5 Sharing your simulations with others
If you make use of our model, please open an issue and let us know. We can add a section on applications and publications to allow modelers to connect and learn from one another.
